name: Branch Brook Park
start_event: The Essex County Park Commission, created in 1895 as the first county park commission in the country, took over Newark's reservoir tract that year: the first county park in the United States
planting_note: Swamp and old reservoir on the Morris Canal bank; Olmsted Brothers plan of 1900; extended north to Belleville in the 1920s; the cherry trees were given by Caroline Bamberger Fuld in 1927

name: Weequahic Park
start_event: Bought by the Essex County Park Commission in the late 1890s (the Waverly fairground and its lake); Olmsted Brothers design
planting_note: State agricultural fairground and trotting track (Waverly Fair) from 1866; 32 ha lake, the largest in the county; golf course 1913

name: South Mountain Reservation
start_event: Land bought by the Essex County Park Commission from 1895, the largest of its reservations
planting_note: Second-growth oak forest between First and Second Watchung mountains, logged for the paper mills of Millburn before; Olmsted Brothers plan; Hemlock Falls; Washington Rock, a beacon site of 1780

name: Eagle Rock Reservation
start_event: Acquired by the Essex County Park Commission from 1895 on the crest of First Mountain
planting_note: Wooded ridge with the lookout over Newark and Manhattan; Olmsted Brothers; casino 1911; hill climb course of 1901-04

name: Verona Park
start_event: The Essex County Park Commission bought the mill pond (Verona Lake) and its banks about 1920; Olmsted Brothers design
planting_note: Mill pond on the Peckman River dammed in 1814, a boating resort from the 1890s

name: Military Park
start_event: Laid out as the Training Place, the militia drill ground of the Newark town plan of 1667; a town park from 1869
planting_note: Triangle on Broad Street; Wars of America monument by Gutzon Borglum 1926; underground garage 1960; restored 2014

name: Mount Pleasant Cemetery
start_event: Newark's rural cemetery on the Passaic, opened in 1844 (the outline of that name in Newark; another Mount Pleasant Cemetery lies in Westchester)
planting_note: Farmland above the river; Gothic gate 1877

name: Fairmount Cemetery
start_event: Opened in 1855 on the western edge of Newark
planting_note: Farmland on the South Orange road

name: Liberty State Park
start_event: Opened on Flag Day, 14 Jun 1976, as New Jersey's bicentennial gift to the nation, on the abandoned yards of the Central Railroad of New Jersey and the Lehigh Valley
planting_note: Made land: tidal flats of Communipaw Cove filled for the railroad terminals between the 1860s and the 1920s (Black Tom lies inside it); terminal of 1889 restored; the interior was fenced off for decades because of chromium fill

name: Lincoln Park
start_event: West Side Park, the first park of the Hudson County Park Commission, opened in 1905 in Jersey City; renamed Lincoln Park in 1930 (several outlines in the region carry this name: this row is the one in Jersey City)
planting_note: Upland on the Bergen ridge and, across the highway, marsh of the Hackensack filled from the 1900s; designed by Daniel W. Langton and Charles N. Lowrie; Lincoln statue by James Earle Fraser 1930

name: Stephen R. Gregg Bayonne Park
start_event: Hudson County park on Newark Bay, laid out by Charles N. Lowrie and opened about 1916
planting_note: Bluff and filled shore of Newark Bay

name: North Hudson Park
start_event: Hudson County bought the woods around Woodcliff Lake in North Bergen in 1908-1910 (James J. Braddock North Hudson County Park)
planting_note: Wooded top of the Palisades with a 6 ha lake

name: Holy Name Cemetery
start_event: Catholic cemetery of Jersey City, opened in 1866 (year not found in the cited article)
planting_note: Farmland on the west slope of Bergen Hill

name: Palisades Interstate Park
start_event: The Palisades Interstate Park Commission was created in 1900 to stop the quarrying of the cliffs; the park was dedicated on 27 Sep 1909 during the Hudson-Fulton Celebration (year not found in the cited article)
planting_note: Cliff foot and talus woods; the trap-rock quarries were bought out from 1900 with J. P. Morgan's help; bathing beaches and boat basins 1910s-1940s; the Palisades Interstate Parkway runs along the top on land given by John D. Rockefeller Jr. in 1933

name: Overpeck Park
start_event: Bergen County park on Overpeck Creek, on meadow given by Teaneck, Leonia, Palisades Park and Ridgefield Park in the 1950s; the last areas opened on a capped landfill in 2010
planting_note: Tidal marsh of Overpeck Creek, diked, dredged into a lake and filled with refuse from the 1950s

name: Van Saun County Park
start_event: Bergen County bought the Van Saun farm in 1957; the park and its zoo opened in 1960
planting_note: Farm on the Paramus-River Edge line; Washington Spring, where the Continental Army camped in September 1780

name: Saddle River County Park
start_event: Chain of parks along the Saddle River from Ridgewood to Rochelle Park assembled by Bergen County from the 1960s
planting_note: Flood plain of the Saddle River; mill ponds; Easton Tower (1900)

name: Garret Mountain Reservation
start_event: Acquired by the Passaic County Park Commission (created in 1927) around 1930; Olmsted Brothers plan
planting_note: Summit of First Watchung Mountain above Paterson; Lambert Castle (1892-93) and its tower (1896) stand on the slope

name: Eastside Park
start_event: Paterson bought its first two parks, Eastside and Westside, in 1888-89 (the outline of that name in Paterson)
planting_note: Hillside above the Passaic; the mansion district of the silk manufacturers grew around it

name: Ringwood State Park
start_event: The Hewitt family gave Ringwood Manor and its grounds to the state in 1936; Skylands and Shepherd Lake were added in the 1960s
planting_note: Ironworks and charcoal woods from 1742 (Ringwood Company, Peter Hasenclever, Robert Erskine, then Cooper and Hewitt); the forest has grown back since the furnaces went out

name: Cedar Lawn Cemetery
start_event: Paterson's rural cemetery, opened in 1867
planting_note: Farmland on the Passaic below Dundee Lake

name: Warinanco Park
start_event: First large park of the Union County Park Commission (created in 1921), designed by Olmsted Brothers; built 1923-1925
planting_note: Farmland and brook hollow on the Elizabeth-Roselle line; lake dug for the park

name: Watchung Reservation
start_event: The Union County Park Commission began buying the valley between First and Second Watchung mountains in the early 1920s
planting_note: Second-growth forest; mill village of Feltville (1845, the Deserted Village) and Lake Surprise on Blue Brook inside it; copper mine of the 18th century

name: Evergreen Cemetery
start_event: Rural cemetery on the Elizabeth-Hillside line, opened in 1853 (two outlines in the region carry this name: this row is the one in Hillside) (year not found in the cited article)
planting_note: Farmland

name: Rye Playland
start_event: Opened on 26 May 1928 by the Westchester County Park Commission, which had bought out the Rye Beach and Paradise Park amusement resorts: the first planned amusement park in the country
planting_note: Beach and salt marsh of Manursing; Art Deco plan by Walker and Gillette with an 80-acre lake and boardwalk; Dragon Coaster 1929

name: Saxon Woods Park
start_event: Woodland bought by the Westchester County Park Commission in the mid-1920s along the Mamaroneck River and the Hutchinson River Parkway
planting_note: Second-growth forest; golf course 1931, the large pool 1933

name: Tibbetts Brook Park
start_event: Opened in 1927, one of the first developed parks of the Westchester County park system
planting_note: Valley of Tibbetts Brook in Yonkers, with the Old Croton Aqueduct on its west side and the Putnam Division railroad through it; lakes and pool of 1927

name: Kensico Dam Plaza
start_event: Plaza laid out below the Kensico Dam, finished in 1917; a Westchester County park since 1963
planting_note: Valley of the Bronx River; the granite for the dam came from a quarry beside it; the village of Kensico lies under the reservoir

name: Rockefeller State Park Preserve
start_event: Given to the state by the Rockefeller family in 1983 out of their Pocantico Hills estate
planting_note: Fields and woods of the estate bought up by John D. Rockefeller from 1893, with his carriage roads; Swan Lake

name: Croton Point Park
start_event: Westchester County bought the point in 1923-24
planting_note: Peninsula of the Hudson: Kitchawank village site, 19th-century vineyards and brickyards of the Underhill family; the county's landfill covered its marsh from 1927 to 1986 and was capped as a meadow

name: Ward Pound Ridge Reservation
start_event: Westchester County bought the farms of the reservation in 1925; it was opened in 1938 after Civilian Conservation Corps work
planting_note: Some thirty abandoned hill farms reverting to forest; named in 1938 for William L. Ward

name: Glen Island Park
start_event: Westchester County bought the island in 1923-24; the Glen Island Casino opened in 1930
planting_note: John H. Starin's summer resort from 1879 to 1904, on five islands joined by fill; the castle of his "Little Germany" survives

name: Sleepy Hollow Cemetery
start_event: Founded in 1849 as Tarrytown Cemetery beside the Old Dutch Church burying ground; renamed at Washington Irving's wish
planting_note: Hillside above the Pocantico River

name: Kensico Cemetery
start_event: Founded in 1889 on the Harlem Railroad, when Manhattan's cemeteries were filling up
planting_note: Farmland at Valhalla

name: Gate of Heaven Cemetery
start_event: Catholic cemetery opened in 1917 at Hawthorne, next to Kensico Cemetery (several outlines in the region carry this name: this row is the one in Mount Pleasant, Westchester)
planting_note: Farmland

name: Ferncliff Cemetery
start_event: Founded in 1902 at Hartsdale
planting_note: Farmland on Secor Road

name: Untermyer Park and Gardens
start_event: The core of Samuel Untermyer's Greystone gardens became a Yonkers city park in 1946, six years after his death
planting_note: Gardens designed from 1916 by William Welles Bosworth on the Tilden estate above the Hudson; walled Persian garden restored since 2011

name: Harriman State Park
start_event: Mary Averell Harriman gave 10,000 acres and one million dollars in 1910 on condition that the state give up the prison it was building at Bear Mountain
planting_note: Cut-over iron-furnace woods of the Ramapo Highlands; thirty-odd lakes, most of them dammed by the park; the Rockland part is the south-east of the park

name: Bear Mountain State Park
start_event: Opened in 1913 on the site cleared for the prison, with a steamboat dock; Bear Mountain Inn 1915, Bear Mountain Bridge 1924
planting_note: Hessian Lake and the ruins of Fort Clinton (1777); the hamlet of Doodletown inside it was bought out by 1965

name: Hook Mountain State Park
start_event: The Palisades Interstate Park Commission began buying out the quarries of Hook Mountain in 1911
planting_note: Trap-rock quarries along the river, the last closed about 1920; ice-house landing of Rockland Lake

name: Nyack Beach State Park
start_event: Bought by the Palisades Interstate Park Commission in 1915
planting_note: Quarry and stone-crusher landing under Hook Mountain

name: Rockland Lake State Park
start_event: The Palisades Interstate Park Commission bought the lake and the village around it in 1958; the park opened in the 1960s
planting_note: Ice-harvesting village of the Knickerbocker Ice Company (1831-1924), cleared for the park

name: High Tor State Park
start_event: Bought in 1943 by public subscription to save the summit from quarrying, after Maxwell Anderson's play High Tor
planting_note: Summit of the Palisades ridge; Revolutionary beacon site; the Van Orden farm and vineyards on its slope

name: Tallman Mountain State Park
start_event: Bought by the Palisades Interstate Park Commission in 1928
planting_note: Palisades cliff above the Piermont marsh; the berms in the woods were built for an oil tank farm of the 1920s that was never finished

name: Blauvelt State Park
start_event: The state rifle range of 1910 (Camp Bluefields) was given up and handed to the Palisades Interstate Park Commission in 1913
planting_note: The concrete walls and tunnels of the rifle range stand in the woods

name: Stony Point Battlefield State Historic Site
start_event: Opened as a state reservation in 1902 on the site of the fort stormed by Anthony Wayne in 1779
planting_note: Rocky point with the lighthouse of 1826; earthworks of the British fort

name: Oak Hill Cemetery
start_event: Rural cemetery of Nyack, founded in 1848 (year not found in the cited article)
planting_note: Hillside above the village

name: Jones Beach State Park
start_event: Opened on 4 Aug 1929, the showpiece of Robert Moses's Long Island State Park Commission
planting_note: Barrier beach raised some four metres with forty million cubic yards of sand pumped from the bay; planted with beach grass by hand; water tower and two bathhouses of 1929-31

name: Eisenhower Park
start_event: Nassau County took over the Salisbury Country Club for unpaid taxes in 1944 and dedicated it as Salisbury Park in 1949; renamed for Dwight D. Eisenhower in 1969
planting_note: Remnant of the Hempstead Plains; five golf courses of the Salisbury club (1917-1920s), where the PGA Championship was played in 1926

name: Bethpage State Park
start_event: The Long Island State Park Commission took over the Lenox Hills Country Club in 1934; four new golf courses by A. W. Tillinghast were built as relief work, the Black Course opening in 1936
planting_note: Yoakum estate and the club's golf course of 1923, on the moraine

name: Hempstead Lake State Park
start_event: One of the first Long Island state parks, on reservoir land transferred by New York City in 1925
planting_note: Storage reservoir of the Brooklyn Water Works, dammed 1873; the largest lake in Nassau County

name: Valley Stream State Park
start_event: Brooklyn Water Works land transferred to the Long Island State Park Commission in 1925; the south part became a village park in 1958
planting_note: Watts Pond and the stream of the old water supply

name: Old Westbury Gardens
start_event: Opened to the public in 1959
planting_note: Westbury House (1906) of John S. Phipps, by George Crawley, with its walled garden and allees on the Hempstead Plains edge

name: Planting Fields Arboretum
start_event: William Robertson Coe deeded the estate to the State of New York in 1949; open to the public after his death in 1955
planting_note: Estate laid out from 1913 (Olmsted Brothers from 1918): Coe Hall 1918-21, greenhouses, beeches moved from Massachusetts by barge

name: Sagamore Hill National Historic Site
start_event: Theodore Roosevelt's house (1884-85) was opened to the public in 1953 by the Theodore Roosevelt Association and became a National Historic Site in 1962
planting_note: Farm and woods on Cove Neck

name: Sands Point Preserve
start_event: Nassau County received the Guggenheim estate from the federal government in 1971
planting_note: Howard Gould's Castle Gould (1904) and Hempstead House (1912), then Daniel Guggenheim's estate; Navy training-device centre 1946-1967
